[IBNASHUR-FULL:v16p232/r7] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | reports | An alternative syntax makes كل شيء the second object and خلقه the first: God gave creatures what they need, as in 6:99; the construction permits both readings. | mentions 6:99
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v16p232/r8] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | reports | The scope of كل is either conventional generality limited to things suited to receiving their forms, or distributive generality pairing each thing with its creation, like people mounting their own animals.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v16p232/r9] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Moses' argument asks whether Pharaoh gave each creature its form; Pharaoh knows he did not, so he should infer that God bestowed existence and blessings and believe in Him through this attribute.
[TABATABAI:20:49-79#2/r1] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The verse emphasizes guidance rather than governance because the context is a call to guidance, to which universal guidance is especially suited.
[TABATABAI:20:49-79#2/r2] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · بعضهم | reports | One interpretation takes 'its creation' to mean its counterpart, so God gave each thing a mate, as in the verse about creating pairs. | mentions 51:49
[TABATABAI:20:49-79#2/r3] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · بعضهم | reports | Another interpretation treats 'everything' as kinds of blessings and 'creation' as created beings: God gave his creatures every blessing.
[TABATABAI:20:49-79#2/r4] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · بعضهم | reports | A further interpretation says God gave each thing its sought existence according to its disposition, then guided people to his existence and unity.
[TABATABAI:20:49-79#2/r5] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | rejects | Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī rejects these alternatives as remote from the context and as restricting the verse's wording without evidence.
[TABATABAI:20:49-79/r1] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Guidance means showing a thing the path to its goal or conveying it there; both reduce to connecting it with what it seeks.
[TABATABAI:20:49-79/r2] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Because guidance is unqualified and the only antecedent is each thing given its creation, it means guiding every thing toward the end for which it exists.
[TABATABAI:20:49-79/r3] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | God links each thing's innate powers and instruments to the effects that carry it toward its final end; a human embryo is equipped to become a complete human.
[TABATABAI:20:49-79/r4] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The conjunction 'then' marks rank order: a thing's movement toward its end follows its existence; for bodily beings this unfolding is gradual in time.
[TABATABAI:20:49-79/r5] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | This is universal guidance, not guidance unique to humans: everything is equipped to move toward its own perfection, and God is the guide.
[TABATABAI:20:49-79/r6] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The systems of interaction among things, both particular and universal, instantiate divine guidance and, from another perspective, divine governance.
[TABATABAI:20:49-79/r7]

TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Governance ultimately depends on creation: the one who brings things into being is also the one to whom their existence and attributes belong.
[TABATABAI:20:49-79/r8] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The verse proves God alone is Lord: creating things entails owning their existence, since they depend on him, and owning their governance.
[TABATABAI:20:49-79/r9] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | In response to Pharaoh's evasive question, 'Lord of all worlds' would assert the claim, but 'the one who gave everything its creation and guided it' also supplies its proof.
[TABATABAI:2:21-25#21/r1] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | God owns all things and may grant others only a dependent permission to act; delegated possession never makes its recipient independent of Him. | mentions 3:26, 20:50
[ASAD-NOTES:20:49#n31/r1] ASAD-NOTES, d. 1412 · author | holds | Although Arabic uses the past tense, the sentence describes creation as continuous and timeless, an unceasing present.
[ASAD-NOTES:20:49#n31/r2] ASAD-NOTES, d. 1412 · author | holds | Khalq here includes both a thing's inner nature and the outward form in which that nature appears, explaining Asad's composite translation.
[ASAD-NOTES:20:49#n31/r3] ASAD-NOTES, d. 1412 · author | holds | Asad traces the underlying idea to 87:2-3, among the earliest Qur'anic revelations. | mentions 87:2-3
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p40/r5] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | Every creature receives a form suited to its purpose and instinctive guidance for its needs, sustenance, reproduction, protection, and role in the wider order.
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p40/r6] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | Birdsong and the distinctive forms, colors, scents, and benefits of plants and fruits all point to their Creator, the true Lord.
